paper_metadata.title: Information Extraction meets the Semantic Web: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Survey of Information Extraction in a Semantic Web setting, examining how Semantic Web languages, ontologies, knowledge bases, and tools can improve extraction and how extraction can populate Semantic Web resources. It covers extraction and linking of entities, concepts, and relations, primarily from natural-language text, with an additional overview of markup documents and web tables.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses the semantic gap between abundant unstructured Web information and comparatively limited structured Semantic Web content. Its objective is to consolidate literature at the intersection of Information Extraction and Semantic Web technologies, including methods that extract and/or link entities, concepts, and relations from unstructured or semi-structured sources.

methodology.description: This is a literature survey rather than a newly proposed extraction system. Its review workflow: define section-specific IE and Semantic-Web keyword lists; search their conjunctions in Google Scholar; filter initial results by title/publication type, then abstract, then full paper; extend the seed set through references, citing papers, prominent authors, and newly discovered keywords. The synthesis is organized by entity extraction/linking, concept extraction/linking, relation extraction/linking, semi-structured extraction, and discussion. Within the surveyed relation-extraction literature, the illustrative execution order is entity extraction/linking, relation parsing, property selection/mapping, RDF representation, and evaluation, while explicitly noting that systems need not follow every step or that order.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: Semantic Web resources are central to the survey scope. Included work must make non-trivial use of RDF, RDFS, OWL, SKOS, SPARQL, or a resource founded on those standards. Ontologies and knowledge bases can guide extraction and be populated by the extracted results; the survey repeatedly uses DBpedia, Freebase, YAGO, Wikipedia-derived resources, WordNet, and domain ontologies as examples.

input_output.input_type: Primarily unstructured natural-language text; additionally semi-structured markup documents and web tables.
input_output.input_granularity: The surveyed methods operate at mention, sentence, paragraph/document, corpus, Web page, markup-document, and table levels; the survey's principal examples use text mentions within sentences and documents.
input_output.output_representation: The surveyed systems output extracted mentions linked to disambiguated KB/ontology identifiers, entity/concept/relation annotations, binary or n-ary relations, RDF triples, RDF/RDFS/OWL representations, and populated or augmented knowledge bases. The survey itself produces a narrative synthesis and comparative tables rather than a machine-generated graph.

models_and_tools: No single model or implementation is proposed; this is a survey.
Representative surveyed EEL tools include SemTag, KIM, AIDA, DBpedia Spotlight, SDA, KORE, LINDEN, and WAT.

Representative surveyed NLP/IE components include Stanford NER/CoreNLP, OpenNLP, GATE, Lucene, dependency parsers, CRF and maximum-entropy NER, graph-based collective disambiguation, distant supervision, OpenIE, frame semantics, and discourse representation structures.
Representative surveyed relation systems include DeepDive, Knowledge Vault, FRED, RdfLiveNews, and Fact Extractor.
datasets: The survey does not train or test one new model on one dataset.
It reviews task-specific resources, including EEL datasets such as AIDA/CoNLL, KORE-50, MSNBC, AQUAINT, ACE2004, IITB, and Microposts.

For REL it discusses manually annotated corpora, held-out KB triples, crowd/expert judgments, and challenge data; examples include NYT/Freebase-style distant-supervision settings and OKE challenge resources.
Knowledge bases used as reference/evaluation resources include DBpedia, Freebase, YAGO/YAGO2, Wikipedia, BabelNet, WordNet, and domain ontologies.

metrics: The survey reports that EEL and REL evaluations commonly use precision, recall, F-measure/F1, and accuracy.
For ranked outputs it reports precision@k, mean average precision (MAP), and, for selected topic-modeling work, held-out-set perplexity/log-likelihood.
It emphasizes that metric choice and precision–recall trade-offs depend on the application and that cross-system results require compatible datasets/settings.
baselines: No single experimental baseline is defined because the paper does not introduce a new extraction model. Instead, it summarizes third-party comparative evaluations and challenge events that compare heterogeneous EEL/REL systems; it cautions that a single technique or system does not cover all use cases.
evaluation.setting: Survey/meta-analysis setting. The authors collect and screen literature rather than run a new shared benchmark. They organize comparative evidence by extraction target and input type, summarize evaluation practices for EEL, concept extraction/linking, and REL, and perform a venue/community meta-analysis over 106 highlighted papers drawn from Tables 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

value: The paper synthesizes entity, concept, and relation extraction/linking methods for text and semi-structured inputs, rather than claiming a new state-of-the-art score.

The authors identify a temporal trend: before about 2009, work commonly used domain-specific ontologies, limited-type NER, manually labelled corpora, handcrafted patterns, and linguistic resources; after 2009, work shifted toward general-domain KBs such as DBpedia, Freebase, and YAGO and more statistical/data-driven methods.
They observe a trend toward holistic/collective and joint modeling of within-task and cross-task dependencies, including NER–EL, WSD–EEL, and EEL–REL interdependencies.
Their venue analysis covers 106 highlighted papers; Semantic Web venues account for the largest single area total (39), while the majority of highlighted work is from non-Semantic-Web communities.

For REL, the survey identifies distant supervision as dominant in recent binary-relation approaches, whereas n-ary extraction more often uses linguistic resources such as frame semantics or discourse representation theory and must address RDF/KB mapping.

value: Review-level inference: The survey is broad and structurally useful for a Text-to-KG review because it connects entity, concept, and relation extraction/linking with Semantic Web resource use, RDF representation, and KB population rather than treating these as isolated tasks.

Review-level inference: Its explicit scope and search/screening procedure improve traceability relative to an unsystematic narrative survey, and its comparative tables make heterogeneous systems easier to locate by task, KB, representation, and domain.

Review-level inference: The discussion of evaluation variability and application-dependent precision/recall trade-offs appropriately avoids treating incomparable reported scores as a universal ranking.

value: Review-level inference: Because this is a 2016-era survey, its methodology taxonomy and empirical synthesis predate transformer encoder and LLM-based Text-to-KG approaches; it cannot establish conclusions about those later families.

Review-level inference: The work groups a very heterogeneous body of systems and application settings. Its useful descriptive comparisons do not provide a unified, controlled quantitative benchmark across all methods.

Review-level inference: The survey's scope requires non-trivial Semantic Web use, so relevant text-to-graph extraction work without RDF/RDFS/OWL/SKOS/SPARQL resources is deliberately outside its coverage.

value: The authors state that their keyword-based survey methodology may miss relevant papers; it only includes papers they could find through that methodology.
They note that included scope is deliberately constrained to non-trivial Semantic Web technologies/resources and extraction from unstructured or semi-structured sources.

For REL, the authors state that many approaches do not explicitly address scale and efficiency, most surveyed systems are evaluated only for English, and language-specific NLP components complicate multilingual use.
They state that automated KB-based evaluation is not suitable for precision when the KB is incomplete, and it assumes withheld KB relations should appear in text.

value: Author-stated direction: Continue jointly modeling interdependent extraction/linking tasks rather than optimizing only isolated components.

Author-stated direction: For multilingual REL, replace language-specific components with equivalents in the target language or translate into a supported language, while recognizing that neither guarantees equivalent performance and translation introduces errors.

Review-level inference: A modern successor should preserve this paper's task/resource-oriented organization while explicitly adding transformer and LLM methodology families, provenance/faithfulness evaluation, constrained generation, and reproducible common evaluation protocols.

value: Author-stated: REL remains an active research area; no single technique/system covers all use cases, and selecting an RE strategy depends on binary versus n-ary needs, identifier creation, language, scale, and efficiency.
Author-stated: Reliable evaluation remains difficult, particularly recall and precision assessment in incomplete KBs and heterogeneous representations/settings.

Review-level inference: The paper leaves unresolved how to obtain directly comparable end-to-end Text-to-KG evaluations spanning extraction, linking, schema alignment, graph validation, and updating, because it reports task-specific evaluation practices rather than such a unified protocol.

The paper does not state that source code for a new system is released.
